content.title: Review
content.review:
This paper proposes a method to transfer a language model pre-trained in English to a new language. The approach consists of learning a mapping to the target language via the adversarial of Lample et al. (2018), a new intermediate layer where hidden representations of the input tokens are reordered based on alignment information of an external aligner tool, and a multi-step training process. The model is evaluated on Chinese classification tasks from the CLUE benchmark and Chinese and Indonesian dependency parsing datasets where it mostly performs competitively with a monolingual BERT Base and slightly outperforms multilingual BERT.

Pros:
1. The paper tackles an important setting, the transfer of models to languages other than English.
2. The proposed method performs competitively with a monolingual BERT model while being more efficient to train.
3. The proposed intermediate layer that explicitly incorporates alignment information is novel. 

Cons:
1. Lack of evaluation on other languages. Despite proposing a general framework for cross-lingual transfer, the paper only evaluates on two fairly high-resource languages, Chinese and Indonesian. Given that the datasets used by the authors for evaluation such as the CoNLL-09 and UD datasets cover additional languages and in light of the introduction of recent massively multilingual benchmarks such as XTREME (Hu et al., 2020) or XGLUE (Liang et al., 2020), evaluation on multiple typologically diverse languages is necessary to demonstrate the generality of the proposed method.
2. Missing baselines. The paper mentions two papers, Artetxe et al. (2020) and Tran (2020) that propose methods for the same setting—transferring an English model to other languages—in the related work section but does not compare to them during the experiments. The authors should also compare to a state-of-the-art multilingual model, such as XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020).
3. It is unclear where the benefit of the proposed approach comes from. The multi-step training process employed by the authors trains only on the monolingual corpus of the target language in the final phase of training. Recent work (Pfeiffer et al., 2020; https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00052) has shown that such target language adaptation improves performance significantly over a pre-trained multilingual baseline. I was not able to find an ablation regarding the effect of this training phase, so the improved performance of the model could be due to fine-tuning only on the target language. At the very least, the authors should compare to a multilingual baseline that was adapted in the same way. This phase also makes the approach less general as the model is specifically tuned for the target language and less transferable to other languages.
4. Lack of references of related work. The intro does not provide any references for related work on cross-lingual modeling and the rest of the paper is generally sparse with references of relevant work. For instance, given that the authors employ an algorithm that has been previously used for mapping cross-lingual word embeddings to map contextual embeddings, mentioning relevant work on this topic such as (Schuster et al., 2019; https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/N19-1162/) would be useful.
5. Some passages in the text are unclear or should be supported with additional evidence. For instance, I found the claim that "symbol sets, symbol order, and sequence length [...] are the three challenges of machine translation" hard to justify without additional evidence given the presence of many other big challenges such as understanding semantics and context, resolving ambiguity, dealing with coreferences, etc.
6. Given the page limit of 8 pages, the organization of the paper overall could be improved. Many important pieces of information such as the entire description of triple-phase training and the entire ablation analysis have been moved to the appendix, with no description of the key takeaways in the main body of the paper. Instead, Section 3.1 for instance, which mostly discusses an existing method could be shortened considerably.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable reviews and feedback. We will make further modifications to the paper and hope this can address your concern.

1)	For your concern on the generality of our proposed method: Because our model focuses on the one-to-one migration of pre-trained language models, and our limitation of computing resources makes it impractical for us to do massive migration training in the short term. We conducted experiments in Chinese and Indonesian when the paper was submitted and reported the experimental performance comparison of various BERT and RoBERTa model sizes to illustrate the generalization ability of the method as much as possible. During the review period, we further verified our method in German and Japanese, and we will include these results in the new version. In addition, we will add references to multi-lingual benchmarks, but since our migrated model is not a multi-lingual model, evaluation on multi-lingual benchmarks is incompatible with our model. Our motivation lies in situations with limited resources (limited data, training resources, training time) and making a transfer as fast as possible and with manageable performance loss. Superior performance is only a secondary consideration.

2)	For the concern on missing baselines: Thank you for pointing out that multilingual baselines such as XLM-R. it is not directly comparable due to the difference in training data size, computational resources, and training time. The first thing to note is that performance is not our primary consideration as our model is under a more restricted condition. We do not aim to bring a new SOTA for multilingual pre-trained language models but to provide a new alternative. We will add a multi-lingual baseline XLM to the new version, use the resources used in the migration process for re-training (including the use of TLM and parallel corpus), and compare it with the XLM model we migrated from English to show fairness. For the models of Artetxe et al. (2020) and Tran (2020), since I cannot obtain the computing resources that match theirs, it is difficult to directly compare them at this time.

3)	For the requirements on finetuning on multilingual pretrained language models: Yes, using the target language to finetune a multilingual pre-trained language model can further improve performance, and we will also add such a set of comparisons, but again, the conditions we consider are limited resources and training time with the goal of migrating monolingual pre-trained language models to achieve comparable performance. We do not negate the role of multi-lingual pre-training language models. The strengths of our method are not in improving performance but in dealing with scenarios where a pre-trained language model meets a new language. We will, however, add such comparisons to provide full context for our models’ performance.

4)	Thank you for your suggestions and we will further add these references.

5)	What we need to explain is that the sentence is expounded from the perspective of the formalization from machine learning, and machine translation is regarded as a problem of mapping from language to language sequence, so the difference between sequences is these three. What we claim is that these three differences are the three challenges of machine translation, but not all of them. Thank you for pointing it out, we will add more references and more appropriate wording to this sentence and others.

6)	Thanks for your very valuable suggestions on the paper organization. We will change it accordingly in the updated version.

content.title: No Baseline From The Literature
content.review:
## Summary
Research Problem: Training BERT from scratch for a language is expensive, transferring knowledge from existing BERT could be more efficient.

This paper proposes a set of techniques to transfer monolingual BERT to other languages. It includes adversarial embeddings alignment, MLM loss with unsupervised word-level cross-lingual signal from bitext, and reordering layer. It considers transferring English BERT to two languages: Indonesian and Chinese. It shows reasonably good monolingual downstream performance while more efficient than training from scratch.

## Pros
It presents various components for transferring BERT, and presents ablation study on some of the components and modeling decisions. 

## Cons
1. While it discusses closely related work like Artetxe et al. (2020) and Tran (2020), and certain ablation is presented in the appendix, downstream performance comparison against prior work is not presented. Additionally, while this paper proposes a number of techniques, it’s unclear how much each technique contributes and the necessity of each proposed component. For example, is the proposed adversarial embedding alignment better than the separate vocabulary approach in Tran (2020)? Without grounding this work in terms of prior work in the experiment, it is hard to assess its contribution in pushing the progress on the main research problem.
2. The model description is a bit hard to follow.

## Questions during rebuttal period
- Why pick English BERT as the source model as opposed to multilingual BERT?

## Reasons for score
Overall, I advocate rejecting. While I find the idea interesting, it is unclear whether it is necessary as no apple-to-apple comparison against previous work is presented. Hopefully the authors can clarify and address my concern in the rebuttal period. 
  
## After revision
Thank you for answering my questions! However, I still find that the current version does not fully address my concern. I would recommend the authors include baselines of Artetxe et al. (2020) and Tran (2020), and fine-tuning mBERT in the main table in future revision.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you very much for pointing out some of your concerns and suggestions on this paper.

1)	For the concern on a performance comparison against prior work: In the submission version, we focused more on the overall migration training approach, so there is no comparison between CdLM and the related TLM and BRLM cross-lingual objectives. Thank you for your reminder. We will add this comparison in the updated version on TRI-RoBERTa-base to show their difference and address your concern.

2)	For the concern on contribution of different proposed components: Due to page limit, we put the ablation analysis of each component of the model in Appendix A.6. We mainly proposed three techniques: 1. a new embedding space initialization, whose advantages we studied in A.6 "Effects of Different Embedding Initialization" and 2+3. CdLM and its supporting TRI-Layer, which we studied in A.6 "Effects of Cross-lingual Transfer Learning".

3)	For your interest on adversarial training vs. separate vocabulary approach: We unified CdLM and MLM into a single form so that joint training could be carried out within batches. Instead of alternating CdLM and MLM optimization models, we use joint embeddings and add language embeddings to distinguish the input language. To compare this with a separate vocabulary technique, we will add a variant in the new version to adapt to separate vocabulary training. Specifically, we will forego language embeddings and adopt independent token embeddings. CdLM and MLM will alternately optimize the model.

4)	For why English BERT not multilingual BERT: There are two reasons: 

a. The performance of English BERT is stronger than that of multilingual BERT (according to previous experiments). Our motivation is to migrate the strongest possible pre-trained language model and get the migrated model to maintain the performance of the original model as much as possible; that is, reduces the loss as much as possible; however, according to our experimental performance comparison between TRI-BERT-base and TRI-RoBRTa-base, the original model RoBERTa-base is stronger than BERT-base, and the models migrated also maintain this trend. Therefore, we chose a stronger original model. Of course, our method can also be used to migrate the multilingual language model, multilingual-BERT, and we will include this comparison in the new version. 

b. The migration of a monolingual pre-trained language model is a more practical scenario. In actual language model pre-training research, advanced pre-training language models usually appear in a common language like English first, such as BERT, RoBERTa, XLNet, ELECTRA, ALBERT, etc., and there are relatively few multi-lingual pre-trained language models. Monolingual language model pre-training is a more active field, and therefore, its migration is a more practical and challenging scenario, although multi-lingual language model pre-training can cover many languages, if it encounters text in a language not covered by its pre-training, the model fails. This is a typical suitable situation for our method, as ours can more quickly adapt a model to the new language compared to re-training a whole multilingual model.

content.title: It does not bring anything new to the field of cross-lingual transfer learning with pretrained LMs
content.review:
=== UPDATE ===
I would like to thank the authors for their work and effort invested into revising the paper. However, some of my concerns (e.g., comparison to relevant baselines, linking core motivations with the experimental setup) still remain. I'd suggest the authors to start from the revised version and further embed some of the great feedback received from all the reviewers, and produce a stronger paper with a clearer presentation (and a clearer motivation and list of contributions) for some other venue in the future.
===============

This papers aims to tap into the very populated area of transfer learning via pretrained language models (such as BERT, RoBERTa, XLM-R). The main idea is to allow for easy adaptation of pretrained language models in the source language to the target language via the usage of parallel data (integrated into model adaptation through a cross-lingual language modeling (CdLM) objective), without the need to retrain the whole model from scratch. In other words, the idea seems to leverage some cross-linguistic similarities to perform better on target language tasks, while keeping the costs of pretraining manageable. Overall, while the paper does an okay work in describing the main idea, profiling the new model in a range of tasks (in two languages only though), and running side experiments and ablation studies, I have several major concerns with the paper, and I am unsure what exact novelty and true contributions this paper brings.

1. Limited novelty A. The main idea largely resembles the idea behind cross-lingual LM pretraining implemented for the XLM model. While the authors do discuss some minor difference to XLM's TLM objective in the appendix, this must be scrutinized more carefully. I am also unsure why the authors never compare to bilingual XLMs for their target languages, and it remains unanswered why this particular model should be preferred over some existing solutions based on XLM, XLM-R, etc.

2. Limited novelty B; missing baselines and related work. The fact that 'bilingual tying' of pretrained LMs (both monolingual and multilingual ones) can be improved by leveraging some bilingual signal: e.g., see the work of Cao et al. (ICLR 2020), K et al. (ICLR 2020), Mulcaire et al. (CoNLL 2019), Liu et al. (CoNLL 2019), among others. However, the paper does not recognise and does not compare to this line of work at all. Therefore, leveraging parallel data as the signal for quick adaptations of pretrained LMs is definitely not new. The paper should discuss previous work adequately and also compare to these approaches leveraging parallel data. 

3. Inconclusive results. Besides lacking several baseline models, even the provided comparisons do not really show the core benefits of the proposed approach - the results, if at all, are only marginally above baselines (from BERT and m-BERT). Considering that recent larger models (such as XLM-R) offer even stronger results on a range of well established tasks, I wonder if these marginal improvements would be visible in that setup as well. Even the argument on the 'economic benefits' (from Table 4) does not hold completely - given training times, why should one opt for the new approach instead of training target-language models such as RoBERTa, XLNet or ELECTRA directly? I fail to see a true benefit here. Further, given that some previous work on improving/aligning monolingual and multilingual LMs applies the 'transfer adaptation' post-hoc (i.e., after training), the whole argument is even more fragile. 

4. A small number of target languages. Given recent evaluation initiatives in cross-lingual transfer learning (e.g., the work on XTREME and XGLUE benchmarks, not cited at all), I wonder why the authors do not provide a wider-scale evaluation on a larger set of languages. This would also allow the authors to analyse the benefits of their method (which takes into account vocabulary alignment and order information) with respect to different target languages and their properties.

As said, while the paper works on a very important problem, I currently do not see it delivering anything beyond what already exists in this crowded area, and minor and inconsistent improvements over an incomplete set of baselines fail to fully convince the reader on the efficacy and usefulness of the proposed method.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1-1
content.comment:
Thanks for your review and suggestions. I respectfully disagree with your comment that this work brings nothing new to the field of cross-lingual transfer learning with pre-trained LMs but also acknowledge in retrospect that our paper had some confusing parts. I hope my clarification here can help you to have a more thorough understanding of our work.


First, it needs to be clarified that the focus of our research is to further the transfer training of trained monolingual pre-trained contextualized language models so that they can adapt to new languages. It does not use traditional cross-lingual transfer learning methods such as XLM’s TLM, where the model is fed a concatenation of the source and target sentences; rather, our model is fed only the source sentence and tasked with predicting tokens in the target language – this is our CdLM objective: a traditional language modeling objective, albeit across languages. We use this objective to train two half-models in opposing directions (source to target and target to source) using our parallel corpora. These models are simultaneously further enhanced with a traditional MLM objective, where they are tasked with predicting masked target or source sentences, respectively. Combining these two half-models, facilitated by our TRILayer, then produces our goal language model. So while we do also use parallel corpora for our method, our objective is fundamentally distinct from that of XLM and others. 

Regarding the first point, what we are exploring in this work is a new method of how to make full use of the existing monolingual pre-trained language models to quickly migrate to a new language at low cost. Because we are using less data and shorter training times, this work does not aim to compete with the strongest multilingual pre-trained language models or monolingual pre-trained language models trained from scratch. To rephrase our contributions: we propose a novel approach to migrate existing monolingual pre-training language models, presenting an alternative to the use of multilingual models. In this approach, we re-initialize our embedding layer using a new joint vocabulary.  We then train the model using a novel cross-lingual modeling objective, CdLM, and an intermediary layer and concatenating half-models. Compared to previous cross-language modeling objectives, such as TLM and BRLM, CdLM aims to migrate models more quickly using explicit alignment signals and minimizing the use of resources for repurposing a pre-trained language model to a new language.
1)	Regarding limited novelty A: Thank you for pointing out this important baseline. As mentioned above, we chose not to include multilingual pre-training because we wanted to emphasize transferring an existing model’s knowledge to another from less training, though we now see in hindsight that bilingual XLMs and similar models definitely merit a comparison, which we will add in the upcoming version.
2)	Regarding limited novelty B: thank you for this new baseline, using parallel corpora to enhance multilingual-BERT. In order to better clarify the role of CdLM, I will build a TRI-multilingual-BERT-base model from multilingual-BERT-base and compare it to other works using parallel corpus to enhance them.
3)	Regarding inclusive results: I need to emphasize that our method is a new option in addition to multilingual pre-trained language models. Our method aims to quickly migrate existing models and make full use of existing pre-trained models. Compared to multilingual PrLMs, our method has a wider range of adaptability. Multilingual language model pre-training requires that all languages are known and added in the pre-training stage. So to add an additional language, a multilingual PrLM must be pre-trained from scratch again. In addition, our work aims to aid in situations where pre-training time and resources are limited ( situations all too familiar to many researchers), especially low-resource language scenarios; the premise of our work is to achieve the best possible results under limited resources. We admit that, if the resources are not limited, it is very intuitive that multi-lingual pre-training is not as good as monolingual pre-training which concentrate more on the characteristic of the specific language.

replying_to: Replying to Response to AnonReviewer1-1

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1-2
content.comment:
4)	Regarding the small number of languages: Thank you for your interest in more languages. We will also cite and discuss the work on XTREM and XGLUE you mentioned. As explained above, we are doing cross-lingual migration from monolingual models, instead of multi-lingual models.  Our current goal is to do a one-to-one migration quickly and efficiently. Because of our current resource conditions, we only trained and evaluated our selection of models in two languages at the time of submission, though during the review period, we additionally completed German and Japanese, and we will report the results in these two languages in the updated version.

Thank you again for your review. Although multi-lingual pre-trained language models such as XLM-R are quite strong, XLM-R cannot handle new language situations in the way that our method can, and we are trying more languages and more types of pre-trained language models. Our method does not transfer learning from traditional multilingual PrLMs but rather provides an alternative option to this. We admit that if the target language resources are sufficient and of high quality, we cannot surpass monolingual models or even those pre-trained in a multilingual setting, but this is not the case for all languages, like low-resource languages, and not all users/institutions have the resources to re-train models. Although everyone can do downstream work following big companies, providing means to make research more accessible is still important for academic prosperity, and we feel our work helps in that regard. Lastly, so far, multilingual models are not as populously researched as monolingual models in languages like English, so our method also offers an option of more quickly harnessing the strength of the latest models.

The strengths and limitations of our work are also very clear. Fast migration with minimal performance loss. Your comments have assumed "adequate training time given" and "adequate pre-training resources including data and computation". In addition, you mentioned that there has been work on transfer adaptation before, but it does not mean that our method has lost its meaning, instead we improved this pattern, and proposed something new and our new method has less performance loss compared to theirs.


> A small number of target languages. Given recent evaluation initiatives in cross-lingual transfer learning (e.g., the work on XTREME and XGLUE benchmarks, not cited at all), I wonder why the authors do not provide a wider-scale evaluation on a larger set of languages. This would also allow the authors to analyse the benefits of their method (which takes into account vocabulary alignment and order information) with respect to different target languages and their properties.

We added the target languages: Japanese and German, and the results are shown in Table 10. The results show that our method is general.

We wish the above could address your concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Cross-lingual Transfer Learning for Pre-trained Contextualized Language Models
display_title: Intuition makes sense; writing could be made clearer.

content.title: Intuition makes sense; writing could be made clearer.
content.review:
This paper presents a method for transfering a contextual language model from English to e.g. Chinese. First, one aligns the embedding spaces. Then, one trains on the new language (but relying on bitext) and an external word aligner reorders the internal hidden states of the contextual language model to respect the new language's word order. 

Pros:
- I think the general intuition makes a lot of sense: we should indeed introduce reordering into contextual language models when doing cross-lingual transfer. 

Cons:
- I found the paper somewhat difficult to follow. See suggestions below.
- The reliance on bitext is quite a large assumption. As such, I think it's necessary to compare with other methods that more directly utilizes the bitext. Also, it is good that Fig 2 examines the effect of bitext amount on BPW, but it would be more convincing to directly show the UAS, F1, or accuracy results as you have in Tables 1-3. 

Suggestions:

- The main motivation of the paper is not extremely clear. It took me a while to realize that your goal is to transfer an existing English LM to a new language to avoide pre-training from scratch on a new language (this is the pre-training cost vs. migration training cost in Section 5). At first I thought you simply wanted to build LMs in a new language (without this pre-training cost issue), and were more concerned with multilingual transferability issues like those addressed by multilingual BERT and its variants. 

- Contributions should be more clearly delineated. For example, you discuss the adversarial word embedding alignment in the abstract but it is just borrowed from previous work. I would suggest focusing just on the TRIlayer, which is your main contribution. 

- There are many results but the exact experimental conditions were not clear. What were the datasets (and their sizes and characteristics) for the downstream task vs the pre-training task, and how they relate to the models in the tables. For example in Table 1, do TRI-BERT-base, BERT-small, BERT-base, m-BERT-base all use the same pre-trained data? Or is BERT-base and m-BERT-base downloaded, while BERT-small and the TRI-BERT-base have new pretrained data? In general these conditions are unclear for all the experiments, so more clarification would help.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
First, thank you very much for your valuable comments and rigorous attitude.
 
1)	For the concern on bitext: In this paper, we focus on how to quickly and efficiently migrate existing monolingual pre-trained language models. That's why we use limited bitext. If the target monolingual resources are sufficient, and sufficient computing resources and time are offered, it is obvious that pre-training from scratch on only the target monolingual data will be more advantageous. We consider a more realistic situation to be one with limited resources (including data, computing resources, and time), where the existing language model on the common language (like English) can be quickly and economically transferred to the target language. This is the motivation of the proposed structure, objective, and training approaches.

2)	For other methods utilizing the bitext to be compared: We will add a comparison of TLM, BRLM, and our CdLM on cross-lingual model migration in the following updated version based on the TRI-RoBERTa-base model.

3)	For the metric adopted in Figure 2: We will soon update this figure with other metrics like UAS for dependency parsing on CTB5.1 and Sem-F1 score for SRL on CoNLL-09 using the pre-trained language models obtained with different amounts of parallel data.

4)	For the organizational issue of the paper: In order to better highlight the main motivation of this paper, we will re-organize the paper and re-emphasize our motivation in the last part of the introduction. In addition, we will move the secondary contribution (adversarial embedding alignment of the work into the appendix) so that the body part will focus more on the structure, objectives, and training approaches proposed by us.

5)	To clarify and detail our experimental setup: our TRI-BERT -* and TRI-RoBERTa-* all used the same size of training data (2M target language monolingual sentences, 1M source language monolingual sentences, and 1M parallel sentences). BERT-small is pre-trained from scratch only on the target language. In order to ensure the training data size is the same, 5M target language monolingual data is used. Compared with the original model, the TRI-* model only has an extra TRI-layer added and some changes in the embedding layer. BERT-base-chinese and m-BERT-base models were downloaded from the official repository, which adopted training data with 25M sentences, a larger scale than our 5M sentences, and more training steps.

content.title: General Response-1
content.comment:
Thanks for your review and valuable feedback.  Although we have done a series of experiments to cover the details of this study, we realize that we should also include the additional experiments suggested by your comments. PrLM related work casts an unprecedented computational cost for NLP researchers, but we will work very hard and focus our computational resources to accomplish the experiments within the upcoming days  Thank you to all reviewers for pointing these experiments out. We will add them in the next edition of our paper. 

We want to clarify that while our work does fall in the populated category of transfer learning for PrLMs, it is distinct from others in that rather than pursuing raw performance gains, it tackles two key and often overlooked aspects of PrLMs: adaptability and scalability. Our primary concern is designing a process by which a model can transition to any language and do so economically.

Pre-trained contextualized language models (PrLMs) are a revolutionary computer science and AI practice. They learn from massive scaled plain text (larger than any other human-annotated dataset) and produce maybe the largest machine learning models yet known. The largest one, GPT3, has 175B parameters.

PrLMs have been shown powerful by generally enhancing nearly all NLP downstream tasks. Adopting PrLMs has become such a common practice in all NLP related work that it is virtually unavoidable.

However, PrLM training cannot be afforded by most (realistically, nearly all) research groups. Only a few well-funded groups can do the work of training a new PrLM. Training a competitive PrLM generally needs hundreds of GPU-days, or even more than 1,000 GPU-days. This huge computational cost for PrLM development leads to an unfortunate new economy in NLP community: one or a few groups do the initial but large-scale pre-training for the PrLM, and all others just take the remaining tasks that involve computationally affordable fine-tuning.

We know there are thousands of human languages. Re-training PrLMs for each individual seems impossible and unnecessary when considering there is common nature among all human languages.

This is the benefit of our method: unlike multilingual and bilingual models that when encountering new languages, require being wholly re-pre-trained on their massive amounts of data, our method has a substantially cheaper (in terms of both data and computational power needed) process for adapting to a new language, and this works for any language with bitext. Our working mode requires only one central/well-trained PrLM in one language (i.e., English), while all PrLMs on different languages are obtained through light-weight transfers from this English PrLM.

Both existing multilingual modes and our transfer mode operate under the hope that only one PrLM is needed for all human languages. The difference is minor but essential: multilingual PrLMs have to be trained again and again when more and more languages are added, while our transfer PrLM does not pose such an inconvenient and unpractical requirement. Besides, multilingual PrLM scheme obviously ignores the big difference among linguistic resources from different languages, while most languages cannot offer large enough and good enough plain text for the supposed large-scale training and only a few languages like English can do so. Simply putting all texts from different languages into one dataset for PrLM training is latently ineffective and inefficient when ignoring such big data scale difference across languages. 

In summary, our transfer method and multilingual PrLMs are similar in that they both use one PrLM for different languages and save computational power in doing so. They differ in that multilingual PrLMs must redo pre-training whenever adding a new language, whereas our method only pre-trains once before it is able to quickly transfer to any language.

replying_to: Replying to General Response-1

content.title: General Response-2
content.comment:
Lastly, we want to clarify our contributions:

In addition to the general multi-lingual language model pre-training and its upsampling strategy, Our main contribution in this work is providing a second novel solution for low resource languages for adapting pre-trained language models to new languages, which is especially suitable for low resource new languages. Because English is a universal language with abundant resources, advanced pre-training language models usually appear in English. Because of the disparity between resource-rich languages and others, making use of the pre-trained language models in common languages such as English and transferring them to other languages is very valuable.

Specifically, in this paper, we borrowed the adversarial embedding alignment work of (Lample et al., 2018) to linearly align the embedding space of a source language with a target language. While doing this, we experimentally verified that embeddings from non-contextualized word2vec training and PrLMs’ raw embeddings from MLM pre-training share spatial structure similarities, which supports our linear alignment. We put forward a novel pre-training objective, CdLM, and unified it with MLM into a single format, making joint learning possible. In regards to model structure, we proposed TRI-Layer to support language conversion during the CdLM training process. We also proposed a half-model training mode so that the upper and lower parts of the final model can adapt to new language features at the same time.

replying_to: Replying to Cross-lingual Transfer Learning for Pre-trained Contextualized Language Models

content.title: Revision Summary
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their time and thoughtful feedback. Reviewers noted that we tackle an important setting in PrLM (R4), our intuition makes sense(R2), and the proposed approach get reasonably good monolingual performance with higher efficiency than training from scratch (R3), and we dose an okay work in describing the main idea(R1). However, the reviewers also have some curiosity and concern about some of the baseline. To address these concerns, 
based on the helpful suggestions and constructive questions of the reviewers, we made substantial changes to the paper organization, baseline model, and comparisons to related works, and added a migration to German and Japanese to show the generalization ability. We have uploaded a new version in which more clarification and more experiments reviewers asked for were added.

The modification can be briefly summarized as follows:

1. Add a scenario figure to intuitively compare the difference between mPrLM and TreLM (see section 1)

2. Add references to more related works (see section 2)

3. Reorganize the description of the framework, focusing more on the method we proposed (see section 3)

4. Add the comparison of the effects of the multilingual PrLM XLM and TreLM under the same data scale, and discussed them in detail (see section 4 "language structure parsing")

5. Supplement the performance of PrLM migrated under different parallel corpora on downstream tasks (see Figure 2)
6. Add the description of the training details (see Appendix A.5)

7. Add the comparison of different cross-lingual transfer learning objectives: TLM, BRLM, and our CdLM, as well as the comparison of the effects of joint vocabulary and separate vocabulary strategies in our TreLM (see Appendix A.7 "Comparison of Different Cross-lingual Transfer Learning Objectives")

8. Add the TRI-m-BERT baseline model, based on this baseline, we extend our framework to migrate the mPrLMs and compare to the related works on transfer learning built on mPrLM (see Appendix A.7 "Comparison with Cross-lingual Transfer Learning Related Works on mPrLM")

9. Demonstrate the migration effect on more languages (see Appendix A.7 "More Languages for a More Comprehensive Evaluation")
